{{Short description|Binary operation, takes two matrices and returns a scalar}}
{{refimprove|date=March 2017}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Frobenius inner product''' (also known as the '''Double-dot product''') is a binary operation that takes two [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] and returns a [[Scalar (mathematics)|scalar]]. It is often denoted <math>\langle \mathbf{A},\mathbf{B} \rangle_\mathrm{F}</math> or <math>\rm A : \rm B</math>. The operation is a component-wise [[inner product]] of two matrices as though they are vectors, and satisfies the axioms for an inner product. The two matrices must have the same dimension—same number of rows and columns—but are not restricted to be [[square matrix|square matrices]].

It is named after [[Ferdinand Georg Frobenius]].

==Definition==

Given two [[complex number|complex-number]]-valued ''n''×''m'' matrices '''A''' and '''B''', written explicitly as

:<math> \mathbf {A} ={\begin{pmatrix}A_{11}&A_{12}&\cdots &A_{1m}\\A_{21}&A_{22}&\cdots &A_{2m}\\\vdots &\vdots &\ddots &\vdots \\A_{n1}&A_{n2}&\cdots &A_{nm}\\\end{pmatrix}} \,, \quad \mathbf {B} ={\begin{pmatrix}B_{11}&B_{12}&\cdots &B_{1m}\\B_{21}&B_{22}&\cdots &B_{2m}\\\vdots &\vdots &\ddots &\vdots \\B_{n1}&B_{n2}&\cdots &B_{nm}\\\end{pmatrix}},</math>

the Frobenius inner product is defined as

:<math>\langle \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B} \rangle_\mathrm{F} =\sum_{i,j}\overline{A_{ij}} B_{ij} \, = \mathrm{Tr}\left(\overline{\mathbf{A}^T} \mathbf{B}\right)
\equiv
\mathrm{Tr}\left(\mathbf{A}^{\!\dagger} \mathbf{B}\right),</math>

where the overline denotes the [[complex conjugate]], and <math>\dagger</math> denotes the [[Conjugate transpose|Hermitian conjugate]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Horn |first=R.A. |title=Matrix Analysis |last2=Johnson. |first2=C. R. |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |year=2012 |isbn=978-0-521-83940-2 |edition=2nd |location=Cambridge |pages=321 |language=en}}</ref> Explicitly, this sum is

:<math>\begin{align} \langle \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B} \rangle_\mathrm{F} = & \overline{A}_{11} B_{11} + \overline{A}_{12} B_{12} + \cdots + \overline{A}_{1m} B_{1m} \\
 & + \overline{A}_{21} B_{21} + \overline{A}_{22} B_{22} + \cdots + \overline{A}_{2m} B_{2m} \\
 & \vdots \\
 & + \overline{A}_{n1} B_{n1} + \overline{A}_{n2} B_{n2} + \cdots + \overline{A}_{nm} B_{nm} \\
\end{align}</math>

The calculation is very similar to the [[dot product]] of two vectors, which in turn is an example of an inner product.

===Relation to other products===

If '''A''' and '''B''' are each [[real number|real]]-valued matrices, then the Frobenius inner product is the sum of the entries of the [[Hadamard product (matrices)|Hadamard product]]. If the matrices are [[Vectorization (mathematics)|vectorized]] (i.e., converted into column vectors, denoted by "<math>  \mathrm{vec}(\cdot) </math>"), then

:<math> \mathrm{vec}(\mathbf {A}) = {\begin{pmatrix} A_{11} \\ A_{12} \\ \vdots \\ A_{21} \\ A_{22} \\ \vdots \\ A_{nm} \end{pmatrix}},\quad \mathrm{vec}(\mathbf {B}) = {\begin{pmatrix} B_{11} \\ B_{12} \\ \vdots \\ B_{21} \\ B_{22} \\ \vdots \\ B_{nm} \end{pmatrix}} \,, </math><math>  \quad \overline{\mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{A})}^T\mathrm{vec}(\mathbf {B}) = {\begin{pmatrix} \overline{A}_{11} & \overline{A}_{12} & \cdots & \overline{A}_{21} & \overline{A}_{22} & \cdots & \overline{A}_{nm} \end{pmatrix}} {\begin{pmatrix} B_{11} \\ B_{12} \\ \vdots \\ B_{21} \\ B_{22} \\ \vdots \\ B_{nm} \end{pmatrix}} </math>

Therefore

:<math> \langle \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B} \rangle_\mathrm{F} = \overline{\mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{A})}^T \mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{B}) \, . </math>{{Citation needed|date=June 2022}}

===Properties===
Like any inner product, it is a [[sesquilinear form]], for four complex-valued matrices '''A''', '''B''', '''C''', '''D''', and two complex numbers ''a'' and ''b'':

:<math>\langle a\mathbf{A}, b\mathbf{B} \rangle_\mathrm{F} = \overline{a}b\langle \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B} \rangle_\mathrm{F} </math>
:<math>\langle \mathbf{A}+\mathbf{C}, \mathbf{B} + \mathbf{D} \rangle_\mathrm{F} = \langle \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B} \rangle_\mathrm{F} + \langle \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{D} \rangle_\mathrm{F} + \langle \mathbf{C}, \mathbf{B} \rangle_\mathrm{F} + \langle \mathbf{C}, \mathbf{D} \rangle_\mathrm{F} </math>

Also, exchanging the matrices amounts to complex conjugation:

:<math>\langle \mathbf{B}, \mathbf{A} \rangle_\mathrm{F} = \overline{\langle \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B} \rangle_\mathrm{F}} </math>

For the same matrix, the inner product induces the [[Frobenius norm]]

:<math>\langle \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{A} \rangle_\mathrm{F}   = \|\mathbf{A}\|_\mathrm{F}^2 \geq 0</math>,<ref name=":0" />

and is zero for a zero matrix,
:<math>\langle \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{A} \rangle_\mathrm{F} = 0 \Longleftrightarrow \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{0}</math>.

==Examples==

===Real-valued matrices===

For two real-valued matrices, if

:<math>\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 6 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \,,\quad \mathbf{B} = \begin{pmatrix} 8 & -3 & 2 \\ 4 & 1 & -5 \end{pmatrix}, </math>

then

:<math>\begin{align}\langle \mathbf{A} ,\mathbf{B}\rangle_\mathrm{F} & = 2\cdot 8 + 0\cdot (-3) + 6\cdot 2 + 1\cdot 4 + (-1)\cdot 1 + 2\cdot(-5) \\
& = 21. \end{align} </math>

===Complex-valued matrices===

For two complex-valued matrices, if

:<math>\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 1+i & -2i \\ 3 & -5 \end{pmatrix} \,,\quad \mathbf{B} = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 3i \\ 4-3i & 6 \end{pmatrix}, </math>

then 

:<math>\begin{align} \langle \mathbf{A} ,\mathbf{B}\rangle_\mathrm{F} & = (1-i)\cdot (-2) + (2i)\cdot 3i + 3\cdot (4-3i) + (-5)\cdot 6 \\
& = -26 -7i, \end{align} </math>

while

:<math>\begin{align} \langle \mathbf{B} ,\mathbf{A}\rangle_\mathrm{F} & = (-2)\cdot (1+i) + (-3i)\cdot (-2i) + (4+3i)\cdot 3 + 6 \cdot (-5) \\
& = -26 + 7i. \end{align} </math>

The Frobenius inner products of '''A''' with itself, and '''B''' with itself, are respectively

:<math>\langle \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{A} \rangle_\mathrm{F} = 4 + 36 + 1 + 1 + 4 = 46 </math><math>\qquad \langle \mathbf{B}, \mathbf{B} \rangle_\mathrm{F} = 64 + 9 + 4 + 16 + 1 + 25 = 119 </math>
